analysis.title: US Rates Watch: UST long end supply / demand
key_insights: Treasury has oversupplied the long end relative to traditional long-end demand sources. BofA says the November refunding may set the stage for, or see, cuts to 20Y and 30Y auction sizes.

Traditional long-end UST holders (property-casualty insurers, life insurers, private DB and DC pensions, federal pensions, state and local pensions) now own 6.5% of total UST supply excluding bills, near the lowest level since the early 1950s.
Private DB pensions, the largest single source of traditional long-end demand, have declined since the 1980s and now own less than private DC plans.

The UST market has not lacked buyers. Foreign investors (Rest of the World), the Fed, money market funds and asset managers have more than offset falling pension and insurer ownership. BofA says this marginal buyer likely does not demand duration structurally the way pensions and insurers did.

The share of UST debt with 10Y+ maturities has nearly doubled from 8.4% to 15.4%. Treasury has grown long-end issuance since the mid-2010s, guided by models that minimize interest expense and interest expense variability.
BofA says Treasury's model may have missed the shift in traditional long-end demand.

Long-end demand and supply trended together from the mid-1970s until the mid-2010s. Since then, traditional demand has weakened further while issuance has grown. BofA says this has likely contributed to cheaper long-end asset swap spreads.
BofA's stated position: stay long 30Y spreads.

trade_ideas.rationale: Treasury has oversupplied the long end versus traditional demand sources, and the November refunding may bring 20Y and 30Y size cuts.

risk_factors: Long-end demand now depends on marginal buyers (foreign investors, the Fed, money market funds, asset managers) who likely do not structurally demand duration.
Treasury's issuance models may not account for the shift in traditional long-end demand.
vol_and_positioning: BofA recommends staying long 30Y spreads. It links long-end asset swap spread cheapening to the gap between long-end supply and traditional demand (Exhibit 7).
